summary: Defines requirements for encoding X.500 Directory attribute syntaxes into strings suitable for LDAP, then describes a string encoding for common syntaxes. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 3494.

plainLanguage.summary: How different kinds of facts in a directory, such as names or numbers, are written down as text.

questions: how are ldap attribute values encoded
how is a boolean encoded in ldap
subtitle: How LDAP writes down X.500 directory attribute values as plain strings, from names and numbers to certificates.

tldr.problem: LDAP requires attribute values to be octet strings, but the X.500 Directory defines attribute syntaxes that are not strings.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets general requirements for string encodings and then gives an encoding rule, often a small BNF grammar, for each standard attribute syntax.
tldr.outcome: This RFC is Historic. It obsoleted RFC 1488, was updated by RFC 2559 and was replaced by RFC 3494.

today: RFC 1778 is Historic. It was updated by RFC 2559 and replaced by RFC 3494. It obsoleted RFC 1488.

sections.title: Encoding Requirements
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) requires that AttributeValue fields be octet strings. RFC 1778 sets the requirements for rules that render X.500 Directory attribute syntaxes into that form, and then defines rules for the standard syntaxes.

Every encoding rule must produce octet strings. Where possible, encoded strings should be usable in their native form for display, so non-binary values should need little or no translation by clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory facts have to be written as plain text. The text should be easy to read as it is.

sections.title: Simple String Syntaxes
sections.content:
Many syntaxes are encoded as the string value itself. This covers Case Ignore String, Case Exact String, Printable String, Numeric String, Octet String, Case Ignore IA5 String, IA5 String and T61 String. Telephone numbers are encoded as Printable Strings, and UTC Time values as Printable Strings holding a UTCTime value.

An Undefined value is encoded as an Octet String holding the BER-encoded value. Passwords are encoded as Octet Strings. Photos are octet strings holding JPEG images in JFIF format, and Fax values are octet strings holding Group 3 fax images.
sections.plainLanguage: Most plain text facts are simply written as they are, with no tricks.

sections.title: Structured Syntaxes in BNF
sections.content:
Other syntaxes use small grammars. Case Ignore List and Case Exact List join strings with a $. A Boolean is TRUE or FALSE, and an Integer is written in decimal digits.

An Object Identifier may be a descriptor, a descriptor with a numeric part, or a numeric OID. Descriptors are preferred where known: for example, organizationName is preferable to ds.4.10, which is preferable to 2.5.4.10.

Telex numbers, teletex terminal identifiers, facsimile numbers, search guides, postal addresses, delivery methods, other mailboxes and mail preferences each have their own grammar. For example, a Mail Preference is one of NO-LISTS, ANY-LIST or PROFESSIONAL-LISTS.
sections.plainLanguage: Facts with several parts, like a fax number plus settings, are written with a dollar sign between the parts.

sections.title: Certificates and Related Syntaxes
sections.content:
A user certificate is encoded as one string with the fields separated by a hash sign: version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, public key information and the encrypted signature value. A CA certificate is encoded the same way.

Authority and certificate revocation lists, and cross certificate pairs (marked forward: and reverse:), reuse these pieces. Distinguished Names and Presentation Addresses use the representations defined in other documents, and the Distribution List Submit Permission has its own grammar with labels such as individual and pattern.
sections.plainLanguage: A certificate has many parts. They are written one after another with a hash sign between each, like items on a checklist.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The RFC states only that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It does acknowledge that many of the encodings are adapted from those used in the QUIPU X.500 implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper does not talk about safety at all.
